title: At the restaurant, and plurals
goal: Ordering a full meal for a group — and making peace with Arabic plurals, which you don't build but memorize.
bekal: ordering food for several people and handling the bill
recognizing the four most common plural patterns
saying what food you like and don't like

dialogs.title: حوار — كشري وسط البلد
dialogs.intro: Budi, Mona, and two classmates have dinner at a famous koshari place Downtown. The waiter shouts from behind the till.

lines.speaker: منى:
lines.id: Four. Is there a free table?

lines.speaker: الجرسون:
lines.text: اتفضلوا جوه. الترابيزة اللي جنب الشباك.
lines.baca: itfaḍḍalu gguwwa. it-tarabēza lli ganb ish-shibbaak.
lines.id: Come on in. The table by the window.
lines.literal: please you(pl) inside. the-table that next-to the-window.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: شكراً. عندكم كشري بس ولا حاجات تانية؟
lines.baca: shukran. ‘anduku kushari bas walla hagaat tanya?
lines.id: Thanks. Do you only have koshari, or other things too?
lines.literal: thanks. with-you(pl) koshari only or things other?

lines.speaker: الجرسون:
lines.text: عندنا كشري وسلطات وحمام محشي وحلويات.
lines.baca: ‘andina kushari wi salaṭaat wi hamaam mahshi wi halaweyyaat.
lines.id: We've got koshari, salads, stuffed pigeon, and desserts.
lines.literal: with-us koshari and salads and pigeon stuffed and sweets.

lines.speaker: منى:
lines.text: أربع أطباق كشري كبير، من فضلك.
lines.baca: arba‘ aṭbaa’ kushari kibiir, min faḍlak.
lines.literal: four plates koshari large, from your-kindness.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: وممكن كمان طبق سلطة وتلات عصيرات؟
lines.baca: wi mumkin kamaan ṭaba’ salaṭa wi talat ‘aṣiiraat?
lines.id: And could we also have a salad and three juices?
lines.literal: and possible also plate salad and three juices?

lines.speaker: الجرسون:
lines.text: حاضر. الشطة على الترابيزة، والدقة كمان.
lines.id: Sure. The chili sauce is on the table, and the vinegar sauce too.
lines.literal: ready. the-chili on the-table, and the-vinegar-sauce also.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: Is the chili sauce very hot?

lines.speaker: منى:
lines.id: A bit. Do you like spicy food?

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: بحبه أوي! احنا في إندونيسيا بناكل حراق كل يوم.
lines.baca: bahibbu ’awi! ihna fi Indunisya binaakul harraa’ kull yōm.
lines.id: I love it! In Indonesia we eat spicy food every day.
lines.literal: I-love-it very! we in Indonesia we-eat spicy every day.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: أنا جعان جداً. من الصبح مااكلتش حاجة.
lines.baca: ana ga‘aan giddan. min is-ṣubh makaltish haaga.
lines.id: I'm starving. I haven't eaten anything since this morning.
lines.literal: I hungry very. from the-morning not-I-ate thing.

lines.speaker: الجرسون:
lines.id: Here you go, the food's here. Enjoy your meal.
lines.literal: please you(pl), the-food came. with-the-pleasure and-the-healing.

lines.speaker: منى:
lines.text: الله يهنيك. يلا يا بودي، جرب.
lines.baca: allaah yihanniik. yalla ya Buudi, garrab.
lines.id: Thank you. Go on, Budi, try it.
lines.literal: God make-you-enjoy. come-on O Budi, try.

notes: **The word اللي means "who / which / that", and it never changes form.** الترابيزة اللي جنب الشباك (the table by the window), الراجل اللي بيتكلم (the man who's talking). Fusha has six different forms for this; Egyptian has just one, much like English "that".

**The word جعان means "hungry" and agrees with the person**: جعان for a man, جعانة for a woman, جعانين for a group. Its relatives: عطشان (thirsty), تعبان (tired), زعلان (upset), فرحان (happy), مبسوط (pleased).
**The word بجد means "seriously?" or "really".** It works as a short question or as an intensifier: بجد كده؟ (seriously, like that?), أنا بجد مش عارف (I honestly don't know).

**The verb يعجب works backwards from English "like".** الكشري حيعجبك literally means "koshari will please you", with the food as the subject — just like English "please" or Spanish *gustar*. It lives side by side with بحب, which has the normal word order.
**The word شطة is Egyptian chili sauce**, and دقة is the garlic-vinegar sauce that always goes with koshari. Both sit on the table for free. To ask for more: كمان شطة لو سمحت.

**The phrase بالهنا والشفا is answered with الله يهنيك.** If you're eating and someone walks past, good manners say you invite them to join with اتفضل — and good manners also say they decline with بالهنا والشفا. Both know it's courtesy, not a real offer.

grammars.title: The four most common plural patterns
body: Arabic has two kinds of plural: one made by adding an ending, and one made by reshuffling the inside of the word. The second kind is far more common, and you have to learn it together with the singular.
after: The reassuring news: you **don't need to be able to build** plurals. What you need is to recognize them when you hear them, and to memorize the plurals of the words you use often. Native speakers memorize them too; nobody derives them from rules.
Even better news: **plurals of things are treated as feminine singular**. So it's الكتب دي حلوة, not حلوين. This rule cuts the agreement problem in half.
For people, agreement is normal: المدرسين دول كويسين. So the only question to ask each time is: is this plural a thing or a person?

grammars.title: Like, dislike, and prefer
body: The verb حب is one of the most used verbs of all, and it covers a wide range — from "like" to "love".
after: Look at row four: after بحب, the next verb stands **without بـ** — بحب آكل, not بحب باكل. It's the same pattern as عايز and لازم in unit six, and it gets the full treatment in unit thirteen.
The phrase مش بتاعي sounds very Egyptian and is very useful. Literally "not mine", it means "not my thing" — a polite way to turn something down without saying you dislike it.

blocks.text: Here too, notice how many words you may already know: لحم، سمك، بيض، رز، ملح، زيت — if you've studied any Arabic, or eaten at a Middle Eastern restaurant, several will ring a bell. Only a few are truly new, and most of those are the names of Egyptian dishes.

blocks.title: Taste and condition of food
items: Taste: حلو *hilw* (sweet), مالح *maalih* (salty), حامض *haamiḍ* (sour), مر *murr* (bitter), حراق *harraa’* (spicy).
Condition: سخن (hot), ساقع (cold), طازة *ṭaaza* (fresh), بايت *baayit* (stale, yesterday's), مستوي *mistiwi* (cooked), نيء *nayy* (raw).
If something's wrong with your food: الأكل ده بارد *il-akl da baarid* or ده مش مستوي. Say it calmly; Egyptian waiters almost always replace it right away.

blocks.text: The question إيه اللي حلو عندكم؟ almost always gets you a better result than reading the menu. Egyptian eateries often have one or two dishes they're really proud of, and they love being asked.
